transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I came in because I’ve been having this awful reaction when I’m driving toward Miami and get to those long bridges. As soon as my car reaches one, my chest tightens, my hands grip the wheel, and I suddenly feel like I have to get off right away—even though there’s nowhere to go.
Do you experience this kind of reaction in situations other than driving on bridges?

No, not really. It’s very specific to those long bridges when I’m driving toward Miami. The moment my car gets onto one, I tense up—my chest tightens, my hands clamp down on the wheel, and I feel like I have to get off right away, even though I can’t.
Are you more afraid of something bad happening, like the bridge collapsing, or are you more afraid of having a panic attack or losing control while on the bridge?

It’s more the bridge itself, I think—the thought of being over all that open water. I know those bridges have been there for years, and people drive over them every day, but in the moment the fear feels much bigger than the real danger.
Do you think you would feel the same level of fear if you were a passenger on the bridge, rather than the one driving?

I think it would still scare me, yes. Maybe not exactly the same if someone else were driving, but the fear is really about being on that bridge over all that open water. I know plenty of people cross those bridges every day and they’re not dangerous in any real way, but in my mind it just feels much bigger than that.
Would you say your fear is more about the bridge itself or about being in a situation where you feel trapped and can't easily get away if something were to happen?

It’s more the bridge itself, I think. I understand those bridges are solid and people go over them every day, but when I picture being out there over all that open water, the fear just feels much bigger than the actual danger.
Does your fear of driving on bridges stop you from going to places you want or need to go?

Yes, it does. I’ve started turning down things I’d normally want to do—gallery openings, birdwatching trips, even visits with my daughter—unless someone else can drive me over the bridges. It’s embarrassing, honestly, because I’ve always been the one who planned things and handled the driving myself.
Are there other activities or situations in your daily life that you're avoiding because of this fear?

Mostly it’s those same kinds of things—places that mean crossing the bridges. I’ve turned down gallery openings, birdwatching trips, and even some visits with my daughter if I can’t get someone else to drive me. It bothers me, because I used to be the one who planned all of that and handled the driving myself.
Is your fear of the bridge related to how high it is above the water?

Somewhat, yes, but it’s more the open water underneath than the height itself. I know those bridges have been there for years and people cross them every day, but when I think about being out there driving over all that water, the fear feels much bigger than the actual danger.
Would your fear of being on the bridge be significantly reduced if you were to cross it by a different means, such as walking or taking public transportation?

I don’t know that walking or taking a bus would make it much better. What seems to matter is getting across the bridges at all. Lately I’ve just been avoiding things—like gallery openings, birdwatching outings, even visits with my daughter—unless someone else can take me over. It’s embarrassing, because I used to be the one who planned things and drove myself.
Would your fear of the bridge be less intense if you were just a passenger in a car, as opposed to being the driver?

A little, maybe, if someone else is driving, but I still avoid it when I can. I’ve turned down gallery openings and birdwatching trips, and even some visits with my daughter, unless someone can drive me over those bridges. That’s what embarrasses me—I used to be the one who planned things and drove myself.
Would your fear of being over open water be triggered if you were on a boat, rather than on a bridge?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t been on a boat much, so I can’t say for certain whether it would feel the same. The bridges are what I’ve noticed most.
Would your fear of the bridge be the same if you were walking across it?
I’m not sure, honestly. I haven’t really tried walking across one, so I don’t know if it would be the same or not. The part I know is that being on the bridge is what bothers me.
Would your fear of the bridge be significantly reduced if you were to drive on a similar bridge in a different location?

No, I don’t think a different location would make much difference. I know those bridges are safe enough—people cross them every day—but when I think about driving over all that open water, the fear just feels much bigger than the actual danger.
Would your fear of the bridge be the same if you were on a bus or train crossing the bridge?
I’m not really sure. I don’t ride buses or trains over bridges like that, so I can’t say how I’d react. I just know the driving over open water part is what gets to me.
Would your fear of being over open water be triggered if you were on a ferry?

I don’t know about a ferry, really. What I know is that when my car gets onto one of those long bridges toward Miami, it hits me right away—my chest tightens, my hands grip the wheel, and I suddenly feel like I have to get off, even though there’s nowhere to go.
Would your fear of being over open water be triggered if you were on an airplane flying over water?
I’m not sure. I haven’t really noticed that with airplanes. I don’t fly over water much, or at least I don’t think about it the same way. What I know is the bridge in the car is what bothers me.
Would your fear of being over open water be triggered if you were on a ferry?
I really don’t know. I haven’t been on a ferry in that kind of situation, so I can’t say for sure. The thing I’m sure about is when I’m in the car on those long bridges over water.
Would your fear of being over open water be triggered if you were a passenger on a ferry?

I can’t really say. I haven’t been a passenger on a ferry over open water, at least not in a way that I remember reacting to it. I just know the bridge situation in the car is the one that sets me off.
Would your fear of being over open water be triggered if you were on a boat in the water below the bridge?

I’m not really sure about being on a boat below the bridge. What I can say is, when my car gets onto those long bridges toward Miami, it hits me right away—my chest tightens, my hands grip the wheel, and I just feel like I have to get off, even though I can’t.
